Gambling Addiction: Signs, Symptoms, and Treatment
blocks.html: Gambling Addiction: Signs, Symptoms, and Treatment

blocks.text: Gambling addiction, also called compulsive gambling or gambling disorder, is the inability to stop gambling even when it is causing harm. It is recognized as a behavioural addiction, which means it affects the brain’s reward system in much the same way drugs or alcohol do. The pull is real, and willpower alone is rarely enough to break it.
blocks.html: Gambling addiction, also called compulsive gambling or gambling disorder, is the inability to stop gambling even when it is causing harm. It is recognized as a behavioural addiction, which means it affects the brain’s reward system in much the same way drugs or alcohol do. The pull is real, and willpower alone is rarely enough to break it.

blocks.text: If gambling has taken over your time, money, or relationships, you are not weak and you are not alone. Problem gambling is treatable, and free, confidential help is available across Ontario and the rest of Canada.

blocks.text: What gambling addiction is
blocks.html: What gambling addiction is

blocks.text: Problem gambling sits on a spectrum. Plenty of people gamble now and then with no harm done. Others reach a point where they cannot control how much time or money they put in, and they keep going even after heavy losses. When gambling damages your finances, work, or relationships and you still cannot stop, that is gambling disorder.

blocks.text: It is not really about the amount of money. It is about loss of control. Someone betting small amounts they cannot afford can be in as much trouble as someone losing thousands.

blocks.text: Signs and symptoms of gambling addiction
blocks.html: Signs and symptoms of gambling addiction

blocks.text: Common signs include:
blocks.html: Common signs include:

items.text: Needing to bet more money to get the same excitement

items.text: Trying to cut back or stop and not being able to

items.text: Chasing losses by betting more to win back what you lost

items.text: Lying to family about how much you gamble
items.html: Lying to family about how much you gamble

items.text: Borrowing money, selling things, or missing bills to keep gambling

items.text: Feeling restless or irritable when you are not gambling

items.text: Gambling to escape stress, anxiety, or a low mood
items.html: Gambling to escape stress, anxiety, or a low mood

blocks.text: If a few of these feel familiar, it is worth taking them seriously. The earlier someone reaches out, the easier recovery tends to be.

blocks.text: Why gambling becomes an addiction
blocks.html: Why gambling becomes an addiction

blocks.text: Every win, and even a near miss, releases dopamine in the brain. Over time the brain starts to crave that hit, and chasing it can override judgment about money and consequences. That is why gambling disorder is treated as an addiction rather than a bad habit or a simple money problem.

blocks.text: A quick self-check
blocks.html: A quick self-check

blocks.text: Ask yourself a few honest questions. Do you gamble longer or spend more than you planned? Have you tried to stop and failed? Have you lied about it or borrowed to cover it? Has it caused problems at home or at work? Answering yes to even a couple of these is a sign to talk to someone.

blocks.text: The toll on family and finances
blocks.html: The toll on family and finances

blocks.text: Gambling addiction rarely stays contained to one person. Debt, secrecy, and broken trust reach partners, children, and friends. Family members often carry stress and shame of their own, and they deserve support too. Our family therapy page explains how loved ones can be part of recovery.

blocks.text: How gambling addiction is treated
blocks.html: How gambling addiction is treated

blocks.text: There is no overnight cure, but the condition responds well to treatment. The most common approaches are:
blocks.html: There is no overnight cure, but the condition responds well to treatment. The most common approaches are:

items.text: Counselling, especially cognitive behavioural therapy, which helps change the thoughts and triggers that drive betting
items.html: Counselling, especially cognitive behavioural therapy, which helps change the thoughts and triggers that drive betting

items.text: Support groups such as Gamblers Anonymous, where people share experience and stay accountable to each other
items.html: Support groups such as Gamblers Anonymous, where people share experience and stay accountable to each other

items.text: Treatment for any anxiety, depression, or substance use that often goes hand in hand with problem gambling

items.text: Practical steps like handing money management to someone you trust and blocking gambling apps and sites

blocks.text: Getting help in Ontario and across Canada
blocks.html: Getting help in Ontario and across Canada

blocks.text: In Ontario, ConnexOntario offers free, confidential support 24 hours a day at 1-866-531-2600 and can connect you to local treatment. Self-exclusion programs let you ban yourself from casinos and online gambling sites. Across the rest of Canada, provincial helplines provide similar free services.

blocks.text: Frequently asked questions
blocks.html: Frequently asked questions

blocks.text: Is gambling really an addiction? Yes. Gambling disorder is a recognized behavioural addiction that affects the brain’s reward system. It is not a lack of discipline.
blocks.html: Is gambling really an addiction? Yes. Gambling disorder is a recognized behavioural addiction that affects the brain’s reward system. It is not a lack of discipline.

blocks.text: Can gambling addiction be cured? There is no instant cure, but many people stop gambling for good with counselling, support groups, and the right help. Recovery is realistic.

blocks.text: Where can I get free help in Ontario? ConnexOntario at 1-866-531-2600 offers free, confidential support any time and can refer you to local services.
